name: PAW Protector
firmware_note: Purely passive analog circuit (power-switch and charge-detect ICs) - there is no microcontroller and nothing to flash. The linked GitHub repo holds hardware design files only.
skill_note: Plug-and-play inline adapter; nothing to configure.
build_note: Ships fully assembled, USB-A male to USB-A female.
summary: A passive inline USB-A adapter that physically severs the D+/D- data lines between a phone/laptop and an untrusted charger or public USB port, while still passing up to 2.4A of charging current (with Apple/Quick-Charge fast-charge detection). It is a 'USB condom' - there is no MCU, just power-management and ESD-protection silicon (TPS2561 power switch, TPS2514A fast-charge detect, TPD2E001 ESD array).
honest_take: It cannot detect or warn you of anything - it structurally blocks data regardless of what is on the other end, so don't confuse it with Electronic Cats' own Paw Detector, which actually inspects a cable. The common misconception is that a 'USB data blocker' senses a malicious charger; this one doesn't sense, it just amputates the data pins, which is simpler and arguably more trustworthy but gives zero feedback if you plug it in wrong or the port is doing something exotic like USB-PD data-over-power signaling.
best_for: Charging a phone from an unknown USB port (airport, hotel, conference) with no data risk
A cheap, foolproof juice-jacking mitigation for non-technical users
not_for: Verifying whether a specific cable or port is malicious before trusting it
Any use case that needs data sync while charging

name: Paw Detector
firmware_note: Runs fixed onboard ADC-based anomaly-detection firmware on the CH32V003; vendor states firmware is GPL-3.0 but no dedicated public repo could be located (see research_gaps).
skill_note: Plug the suspect cable/port through it and read one LED - no software, no setup.
summary: A keychain-sized USB pass-through tester built around a CH32V003 RISC-V microcontroller that runs onboard ADC analysis on the data-line pins to flag the electrical signature of a hidden keylogger/exfiltration implant inside a 'malicious cable' (O.MG-Cable-style). A steady LED means the cable/port is flagged as suspicious; no light is the vendor's 'presumed safe' state. Presented at DEF CON 34.
honest_take: This is a heuristic anomaly detector tuned against known inline-implant electrical signatures, not a certified verifier - a well-engineered implant that keeps its data-line loading within normal-cable tolerances, or one that only activates after a time delay, is a plausible way to slip past it, and it only tests the instant you plug in rather than continuously monitoring. The common misconception is treating a clear LED as proof a cable is safe in any absolute sense; it only means this specific detector's heuristics didn't trip, against the implant designs it was tuned on.
best_for: Screening an unfamiliar or borrowed USB cable before trusting it with a laptop/phone
Quick field checks at cons/travel where O.MG-style cable implants are a realistic threat
not_for: Formal / certified cable security auditing
Detecting exfiltration methods that don't rely on an inline active implant (e.g. a compromised charger's firmware alone)

name: USBKeylogger
firmware_note: Arduino-style .ino sketch for the ESP8266; user compiles and flashes it themselves, there is no pre-flashed commercial unit.
price_note: No commercial kit or vendor listing exists. Estimate is parts cost only (ESP-07S module, 3MB+ SPI flash, small PCB, passives) based on typical pricing for boards of this complexity; PCB fabrication and assembly are on the builder. Gerbers and BOM are published on OSHWHub, not sold as a kit.
skill_note: Requires SMD soldering (or a PCB assembly service) and flashing ESP8266 firmware; no case design or enclosure is provided.
build_note: Gerber files and BOM only - two PCB variants (compact inline, and a USB-hub form factor with one logging port). No assembled option exists.
summary: A hardware keystroke logger built around an ESP8266 (ESP-07S) module that sits inline between a USB keyboard and the host, invisible to host-side antivirus because the capture happens entirely in hardware before the OS ever sees it. It logs to 3MB of onboard flash in a circular buffer and can push AES-128-encrypted keylogs over its own Wi-Fi to ntfy.sh or a custom HTTP endpoint; a bundled offline HTML tool decrypts the payload. Ships as Gerbers/BOM only, in a compact inline form or a USB-hub form where only the bottom port logs.
honest_take: 'Invisible to antivirus' is true only for the host machine - the device broadcasts its own open Wi-Fi access point (default SSID USBKeylogger_XXXXXX) by default, which is a dead giveaway to anyone running a Wi-Fi scanner nearby, and unless you self-host an ntfy server, the public ntfy.sh relay only retains pushed logs for 3 hours. This is a real wiretapping device, not a 'pentest gadget' in the softened sense the README's framing implies - installing it on hardware you don't own or aren't explicitly authorized to monitor is a criminal offense almost everywhere (see legal notes), regardless of how the project markets itself.
best_for: Authorized red-team engagements with signed physical-access scope
Learning USB HID sniffing and ESP8266 exfil techniques on your own hardware
not_for: Covert installation on any device/person without explicit authorization (illegal in virtually all jurisdictions)
Long unattended deployments on the default public ntfy.sh relay (3-hour log retention)

name: okhi (Open Keylogger Hardware Implant)
firmware_note: Open-source MIT-licensed firmware for both chips; supports OTA updates over Wi-Fi from v7 onward, so the implant can be updated in place without physical access after initial installation.
price_note: Implant board alone, sold via the rootkit.es storefront (now hosted on Elecrow after rootkit.es/fr33project.org migrated). Required companion probe boards are extra: USB Sniffing Adapter $33, PS/2 Sniffing Adapter $33, PS/2 5V-to-3.3V Level Shifter $23 - a working USB sniffing setup is closer to $122 all-in. It is also fully open hardware/source if you'd rather build it yourself.
skill_note: The implant itself ships assembled and pre-designed for concealment, but wiring it into a target keyboard/tower covertly (tapping cable pads or internal traces) demands real soldering and tradecraft even though the board needs no assembly.
build_note: Sold pre-assembled; fully open hardware (MIT) if you want to fab your own instead. A separate 'implant probe' board (USB or PS/2 variant) is required to program and test it before deployment.
summary: A tiny (implant-sized) RP2040 + ESP32-C2 board designed to be concealed inside a keyboard, laptop, or tower case, intercepting USB (low-speed) or PS/2 keystrokes and serving them over its own Wi-Fi web dashboard in real time. It draws its power parasitically from the keyboard's own cable (~120 mA) rather than needing a battery, persists every keystroke to its own flash so nothing is lost across reboots, and supports OTA firmware updates over Wi-Fi from v7 onward so it never needs to be pulled once installed.
honest_take: The parasitic-power design and OTA updates make this materially harder to detect and easier to maintain than a typical inline keylogger dongle - there's no separate device plugged into a USB port to notice, and updates don't require reopening the target. That is also exactly why it is a serious surveillance/wiretapping tool rather than a toy: unlike a bolt-on USB dongle, it is explicitly engineered to be permanently embedded and forgotten. Treat the 'proof of concept and educational tool' framing in the README as a legal disclaimer, not a technical limitation - the hardware works exactly as advertised for covert, persistent keystroke capture.

Research into USB/PS2 protocol sniffing and RP2040+ESP32 dual-chip OTA design
not_for: Installing on any keyboard/computer without the owner's and every user's explicit, informed consent - a legal minefield almost everywhere

name: HydraLink
firmware_note: Open-source (MPL-2.0) Python CLI plus a separate Linux kernel module (dissecto-GmbH/hydralink-kernel-module) for native low-latency interface support.
price_note: Crowd Supply campaign price; 222% funded as of research date and listed 'Available for pre-order', shipping had begun per a Jul 30 2025 update.
skill_note: Assumes familiarity with Ethernet tooling (Wireshark/tcpdump/bridge-utils) and automotive network concepts (SOME/IP, DoIP); the hardware itself is plug-and-play.
build_note: Fully assembled pocket-sized module, USB 3.0 Gen1 Type-C in, pre-soldered 2.54mm header out to the single-pair Ethernet wires.
summary: A USB 3.0 to automotive Ethernet (100BASE-T1 and 1000BASE-T1 single twisted pair) adapter that enumerates as a native Ethernet interface (hydra0/hydra1) on Linux/macOS/Windows, so standard tools - Wireshark, Scapy, tcpdump, bridge-utils, ethtool - work against in-vehicle Ethernet with no special drivers. Two units, one set to master and one to slave, form a transparent Layer-2 wire-speed MITM bridge for fuzzing SOME/IP or validating DoIP implementations. It has no CAN, LIN, or any other automotive-bus support at all - Ethernet only.
honest_take: This solves a real, underserved gap - almost every other budget automotive tool on the market (including everything else in this batch) is CAN-only, and modern vehicles increasingly run Ethernet backbones that those tools simply cannot see. But 'open source' here is qualified: dissecto states the schematic is redacted because it depends on proprietary information from the single-pair PHY chip vendor, so you get open drivers and firmware, not a fully open hardware design, unlike CANable/CANtact/panda. It also only speaks single-pair automotive Ethernet (100/1000BASE-T1) - it will not talk to a normal office switch or a standard 100BASE-Tx/1000BASE-T link the way the pricier TOSUN TE1051 ($1,642) can.
best_for: Fuzzing/validating SOME/IP and DoIP implementations on Ethernet-backboned vehicles
Building a portable master/slave MITM bridge for in-vehicle Ethernet without bulky media converters
not_for: Any CAN, CAN-FD, or LIN work - it has zero automotive-bus support outside Ethernet
Connecting to standard office/home Ethernet gear (100BASE-Tx/1000BASE-T are not supported)

summary: An open-hardware, dual-channel, galvanically isolated USB-to-CAN interface: one channel is CAN/CAN-FD/single-wire-CAN, the other is CAN/CAN-FD, both behind isolation between the CAN side and USB/host side, over a high-speed (480 Mbit/s) USB link with dual DB9 connectors. It was the professional successor to Eric Evenchick's original single-channel, non-isolated CANtact, and directly benchmarked itself on its own Crowd Supply page against the isolated 2-channel ICS ValueCAN 4-2 ($445) and the non-isolated Tiny-CAN II-XL (~$180).

The Crowd Supply campaign is fully sold out and marked discontinued, so treat any listing you find elsewhere with suspicion; the currently-buyable open-hardware alternative with real isolation is CANable Pro from Openlight Labs, though that one drops CAN-FD to keep isolation, which CANtact Pro did not have to compromise on.

not_for: Buying today - it is discontinued; look at panda (CAN-FD, 3 channels, isolation unconfirmed) or CANable Pro (isolated, but no CAN-FD) instead

name: CANHack Toolkit / CANPico
firmware_note: MicroPython library (canhack.c/canhack.h under the hood) demonstrating low-level bit-banging attacks against the CAN protocol itself; includes a special build for the DEF CON 30 Car Hacking Village badge.
price_note: Last known price for the assembled CANPico board (Raspberry Pi Pico pre-installed) from SK Pang Electronics. The board now appears discontinued: SK Pang's own listing title reads 'CANPico Board - Retired, replacement available' and the vendor's own product page (canislabs.com/canpico/) no longer resolves to working content. The CANHack software toolkit itself remains available and usable on any RP2040 + compatible CAN-FD transceiver combo.
skill_note: This is a protocol data-link-layer attack toolkit (bus-off DoS, selective frame corruption via precise bit timing), not a beginner sniffing tool - it assumes real understanding of CAN's arbitration/error-handling mechanics.
build_note: CANPico shipped as an assembled Pi Pico carrier board; since it's discontinued, the same MicroPython toolkit can be rebuilt on any RP2040 board wired to a CAN-FD controller/transceiver pair (~$15-20 in parts) as a DIY substitute.
summary: A proof-of-concept library demonstrating that CAN's data-link layer can be attacked directly through precisely-timed bit-banging - no cryptographic break needed - to cause denial-of-service (bus-off attacks) or selective corruption of specific frames on a live CAN bus. It ran on CANPico, a carrier board pairing a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040) with Microchip's MCP2517FD CAN-FD controller and MCP2562FD CAN-FD transceiver on a screw terminal, with a MicroPython build also made for the DEF CON 30 Car Hacking Village badge.
honest_take: The real contribution here is the technique, not the board: CANHack proves that CAN's total lack of frame authentication and its cooperative, deterministic error-handling can be turned into precision denial-of-service and selective-corruption primitives using only accurate timing, which is a genuinely important result for understanding why CAN alone is not a security boundary. The hardware it shipped on (CANPico) looks to be discontinued at its original retailer and the vendor's own product page is dead, but because the technique only needs an RP2040 plus an FD-capable MCP2517FD/MCP2562FD pair and runs in MicroPython, it is straightforward to rebuild on generic parts if you can't find an original board.

standalone_untethered.note: Once flashed, the Pico runs the attack/demo code with no host PC required.

usb_mass_storage.note: Standard RP2040 UF2 bootloader behavior: mounts as a mass-storage device for drag-and-drop firmware flashing.

uart.note: Not documented as a general-purpose external UART bridge; RP2040 exposes UART pins generically but this is not an advertised feature of the CANPico board.

glitching.note: Not voltage/clock glitching - the toolkit's attacks are protocol-timing based (bit-banging valid/invalid CAN frames), a different technique from hardware fault injection.

can_sniff.note: The published bus-off/frame-corruption attack technique fundamentally requires precise real-time monitoring of bus state to time its bit-level interference, and the underlying hardware (MCP2517FD CAN-FD controller) is a full CAN controller capable of ordinary receive.

can_inject.note: The toolkit's whole purpose is precisely-timed bit-level interference on a live bus - denial-of-service (bus-off attacks) and selective frame corruption - a more surgical form of injection than plain frame transmission, not less.

can_fd.note: Built on Microchip's MCP2517FD CAN-FD controller and MCP2562FD CAN-FD transceiver - CAN-FD-capable hardware, though the published attack technique itself targets classic CAN framing/arbitration/error-handling behavior specifically, not CAN-FD's different error model.

can_isolated.note: Per this record's own research_gaps: 'No galvanic isolation is mentioned for the CANPico board; treated as unconfirmed/likely absent rather than asserted' - keeping that same hedge here rather than asserting either way.

obd2.note: This is a data-link-layer attack research toolkit, not built or marketed as a vehicle diagnostic tool, and no OBD-II protocol support is documented - though the CAN-FD-capable hardware could physically reach a live vehicle's OBD-II port if wired to it.

legal.notes: Unlike passive CAN sniffing, this toolkit implements active attacks (bus-off denial-of-service, selective frame corruption) against a live CAN network. Using these techniques on a bus you do not own or are not explicitly authorized to test is unauthorized access and/or computer/vehicle damage under most jurisdictions' computer-misuse and criminal-damage statutes, and is more serious than passive monitoring. Research and testing on your own hardware, or under a signed authorization, is the legitimate use case. Not legal advice - check local law.

name: WiCAN
firmware_note: Open-source firmware shared with WiCAN Pro; on this base hardware it supports RealDash, SavvyCAN, BUSMaster, python-can/SocketCAN, and a browser-based Web-CAN client over WebSocket/WebUSB.

summary: An ESP32-C3-based CAN-to-Wi-Fi/BLE bridge sold as either an OBD-II dongle (WiCAN-OBD) or a bare USB/screw-terminal board (WiCAN-USB), supporting CAN 2.0 A/B up to 1 Mbit/s with a built-in web interface for Wi-Fi/CAN configuration, an AP-or-station Wi-Fi mode, MQTT battery-voltage alerts, and a sub-1mA sleep mode triggered by low bus voltage. honest_take: At $42 for either form factor, this is one of the cheapest actively-maintained CAN-to-Wi-Fi bridges around (770 GitHub stars, commits within the last day as of this writing) - but it is CAN 2.0 only with no galvanic isolation and no CAN-FD, so treat it as a telemetry/convenience tool for your own vehicle rather than a lab-grade interface. For CAN-FD, step up to WiCAN Pro or panda; for isolation, step up to CANable Pro.

name: hitager
firmware_note: Windows GUI + Arduino (Nano/Mega2560) firmware; user builds/flashes both sides themselves, no packaged installer or commercial kit.
price_note: No commercial kit exists. Estimate covers an Arduino Nano/Mega2560 only (~$5-15) - it does NOT include a PCF7991-based reader board (e.g. an iProg RFID Adapter, Hitag2 v3.1 reader, or ZedBull Mini), which the project requires but does not sell and which typically costs significantly more than the Arduino itself. Total realistic cost to get a working setup is well above this headline figure.
skill_note: Requires deep familiarity with NXP Hitag2/Hitag3/Hitag AES cryptography and automotive immobiliser systems, plus sourcing and wiring a separate PCF7991 reader board the project does not provide.
build_note: Bring-your-own-hardware: an Arduino Nano or Mega2560 plus a separately-sourced PCF7991-based reader board (not sold by this project). The GitHub wiki includes a 'building your own hitager hardware' guide.
summary: A Windows GUI plus Arduino firmware combination for reading, writing, and cloning NXP Hitag-family low-frequency (125kHz) automotive immobiliser transponders - Hitag2, Hitag2+EE, Hitag2 Extended (including the BMW EE extension), Hitag3, Hitag AES, and Hitag Pro - plus VVDI Super Chip and specific BMW key part numbers (PCF7944/7945/7953). It relies on an NXP PCF7991 Advanced Base Station IC, which must be sourced from a compatible existing reader product (examples given: an iProg RFID Adapter, a Hitag2 v3.1 reader, or a ZedBull Mini) since the project does not sell or design its own RF front end.
honest_take: This is a serious, narrow tool for one specific job - attacking NXP Hitag-family immobiliser transponders used across a large share of 2000s-2010s VAG/BMW/etc. keys - not a general RFID/NFC tool, and it has zero HF 13.56MHz capability (no Mifare, no general NFC, no EMV), so don't buy it expecting Flipper-style card cloning. It's also genuinely bring-your-own-hardware in a way the $25 headline cost obscures: the actual RF front end (a PCF7991-based reader) isn't sold by the project at all, so the real cost and difficulty of getting a working setup are both meaningfully higher than the Arduino-only estimate suggests. It has been quiet since a January 2023 last commit, so treat it as a stable-but-unmaintained reference tool rather than an actively supported one.

Cloning/programming Hitag-family keys for vehicles you own, if you already have a compatible PCF7991 reader
